[b]Momentum, Movement & Environmental Flow – Valley’s Unreal Locomotion Playground[/b]

[i]A first-person movement adventure where speed, traversal, and a gravity-defying exosuit turn exploration into pure kinetic expression. [/i]

[b]Core Gameplay & Movement System[/b]  
Valley is fundamentally a movement-driven first-person adventure built around the L.E.A.F. suit, which transforms traversal into the main mechanic rather than combat or survival systems. Running, jumping, and chaining momentum-based movement through forests, ruins, and open valleys forms the core loop. The game constantly rewards speed — the faster and more fluid your traversal, the more expressive the experience becomes. 

[b]L.E.A.F. Suit Mechanics[/b]  
The L.E.A.F. suit is the defining system here. It enhances mobility with extreme speed, high jumps, and environmental interaction tied to life-force manipulation. This creates a dual-layer mechanic: movement is not just traversal, but also tied to how the world responds to your presence. The more you engage with the suit’s abilities, the more you reshape how spaces are navigated. 

[b]Traversal Flow & Level Design[/b]  
Levels are structured as semi-linear environments that encourage fast routing and discovery. Open outdoor spaces emphasize momentum-building, while interior sections slow things down into tighter platforming sequences. The contrast creates a rhythm of acceleration and control — sprinting across massive terrain one moment, then carefully navigating ruins the next.

[b]Life–Death Environmental System[/b]  
A subtle but important mechanical hook is the life/death interaction system. The suit’s power allows manipulation of life energy, and environmental consequences scale with your actions. Even repeated failure subtly alters the state of the world, tying progression and traversal to your performance in a way that reinforces engagement with movement precision.

[b]Exploration & Reward Structure[/b]  
Exploration is built around fluid movement rather than branching systems. Hidden paths, optional traversal routes, and environmental bonuses reward curiosity, but the game never overwhelms you with complex mechanics — it stays focused on maintaining flow.

[b]Pacing & Player Expression[/b]  
Valley’s strongest mechanical identity is its sense of speed and momentum. The game prioritises “feeling fast” over mechanical complexity, letting movement itself become the primary expression of skill. It sits closer to a kinetic platformer than a traditional adventure game, where control mastery is the core reward loop.

[b]Verdict – 10/10[/b]  
Valley turns traversal into its main system, delivering a movement-first experience where speed, flow, and environmental interaction define the entire gameplay identity.

Valley is something of a feathered fish. It's an atmospheric walking simulator and a platformer with FPS elements. However, it is a fish that manages to majestically fly and swim at once, at least when everything clicks together.

If you've ever played a 2010s walking simulator, you know what to expect. Your tossed into a mysterious land with only voice memos (remember those?) and other visual clues to piece together what happened as you journey further into the heart of the valley. However, what sets it apart is that it's a RUNNING simulator, as your new suit allows you to zoom zoom zoom at incredible speeds. Did I mention that you can also do crazy jumps, turning it into a fun platformer? As well as being able to shoot energy beams at malicious spirits and also use your suit to bring everything back to life.

It's a short game, evidenced by my play time (3.5 hours) for one playthrough (and that was me taking my time to scavenge for items). Valley is also a pretty easy game, as health is plentiful, jumping gives lots of mercy to your trajectory, and you're given so many "lives" that you pretty much have to get a game over on purpose. However, I think the easy difficulty fits its laid back atmosphere setting which turns it into the type of game you play when you want to chill for a while.

tl;dr Still worth a purchase when it's on sale.

Valley is a really strange game. On the one hand, it is a perfectly adequate first-person arcade platformer with well thought out mechanics, magic acorns, pixies, and nice visuals. On the other hand, it tries to tell a serious story set during World War II that feels like a parody on Portal, written by a 12 year old. I kid you not, the notes you find spread all over this Sussurian valley are some of the corniest things you will ever read. The result is a game that feels like it was never finished and I honestly can't tell who it was made for. The difficulty is laughably easy as you are constantly fed energy upgrades even though there are infinite energy sources literally around every corner and never given anything challenging to do with all that energy. Enemies are few and far between and die instantly without ever posing any threat. Controls cannot be remapped. Sound volume settings lack a slider for audio tapes and I could barely hear the story advancing recordings behind the music. But worst of all, there is just no point in exploring this beautiful world to find all its secrets because all you get for going off the beaten path is more acorns and suit upgrades, which you didn't really need to begin with. And you don't even get a zoom ability to help look for collectibles in these massive environments. Valley has a lot of unrealized potential but in its current state the story is bad and the journey is just not worth it.

Valley, developed by Blue Isle Studios and published by Blue Isle Publishing, is a first-person adventure that blends exploration, science fiction, and nature’s quiet mysticism into a single sweeping experience. It begins with a sense of isolation and curiosity, placing the player in a remote, mountainous region filled with ancient ruins, forested trails, and remnants of a secret military experiment. The discovery of the L.E.A.F. suit—an exoskeleton designed to grant superhuman speed, agility, and control over life and death—sets the stage for an experience that balances beauty with danger. This premise alone is enough to intrigue anyone drawn to the mysterious allure of abandoned research projects and forgotten landscapes, but what truly defines Valley is how it translates that intrigue into kinetic freedom. The world is alive, breathing, and reactive, and every leap through the lush valley feels like an expression of vitality itself.

At its core, Valley thrives on movement. The L.E.A.F. suit is not just a gameplay gimmick—it’s the key to an exhilarating sense of flow that makes traversal both graceful and empowering. Running through open fields, bounding off cliffs, and soaring across gorges, the player feels momentum that rivals the fluidity of parkour-inspired titles while still being grounded in the game’s somber tone. Each region of the valley feels handcrafted to complement this motion: dense forests give way to meadows scattered with ruins, and narrow industrial corridors contrast sharply with the open natural beauty outside. The world encourages exploration through its verticality and hidden pathways, and although the progression is largely linear, it’s easy to get lost in the rhythm of the journey. The game captures that rare sense of “flow state,” where motion, sound, and sight blend into something almost meditative.

The central mechanic of the L.E.A.F. suit—the ability to both give and take life—adds a layer of moral and thematic tension to the adventure. The suit allows the player to restore dead plants and animals, reviving barren landscapes and rejuvenating decayed ecosystems. But the same power can also be used destructively, draining life energy to sustain oneself or fuel upgrades. This balance between creation and consumption forms the emotional spine of Valley’s experience. Every death carries a tangible cost: the player’s demise results in the decay of the surrounding environment, connecting mortality to the health of the world in a way that few games attempt. It’s a simple mechanic, but its implications are powerful. It encourages the player to think about their relationship to the world, transforming what would otherwise be routine respawns into moments of reflection about consequence and renewal.

Visually, Valley is a quiet marvel. The art direction focuses on mood rather than realism, combining the grandeur of mountainous terrain with glowing flora, ancient structures, and the haunting remains of wartime experiments. The contrast between nature’s serenity and the remnants of human ambition gives the world a melancholic atmosphere. The color palette shifts subtly between warm light and cool shadows, emphasizing the duality that runs through every aspect of the game—life versus death, creation versus destruction, science versus nature. The soundtrack enhances this emotional contrast beautifully. Its orchestral swells and ambient tones react to movement and discovery, often rising in step with your speed and fading during quieter moments, reinforcing the sensation that the valley itself is alive and aware of your presence.

Yet for all its artistry and mechanical charm, Valley’s weaknesses are hard to ignore. Its narrative, told through scattered audio logs and environmental clues, hints at deep lore and philosophical undertones but never fully develops them. The story touches on scientific hubris, environmental ruin, and the moral burden of power, but these ideas remain fragments rather than cohesive arguments. The pacing occasionally stumbles when combat encounters break the fluid rhythm of traversal, and while the suit’s energy mechanics are intriguing, they don’t evolve much over time. The game also ends rather abruptly, just as its world feels like it’s opening up to larger possibilities. This brevity can leave players with a sense of incompleteness, as if the valley still holds secrets it was never given enough time to reveal.

Despite these shortcomings, Valley remains a memorable and emotionally resonant experience. Its greatest triumph is how it conveys the joy of motion and the beauty of its world through gameplay alone, without the need for heavy exposition. Few games manage to make speed and grace feel so intrinsically tied to the narrative’s emotional core. Even when the story fades into the background, the act of running, leaping, and reviving life feels deeply satisfying, as though you are participating in the valley’s healing process. It is the kind of game that leaves an impression not through scale or complexity, but through the quiet strength of its design and the atmosphere it sustains from beginning to end.

Valley may not reach the narrative ambition of its premise, but it stands out as a rare example of a game that makes movement itself a form of storytelling. It is short, haunting, and filled with moments of serene beauty that linger long after the credits roll. Whether you see it as a parable about humanity’s connection to nature or simply as an exhilarating adventure through a forgotten world, it achieves something timeless: it makes you feel alive in motion. And in a story so preoccupied with life and death, that feeling alone is worth the journey.

Having completed the game now, I'd say a review is in order...

The story in itself isn't really that bad. It's very poorly told using Fallout 76 launch tapes instead of actual characters or much of anything else worth note. Most of the game leaves you to find notes and left documents but it all but trains you as a player to ignore them because a good 80-90% of it is filled with information you already knew before you got to the notes themselves or it's inane prattle from characters that don't even make an appearance in the game.

That brings me to the actual game play and the genre. The genre has it classified as exploration and such. Problem is that there is enough "exploration" in the game to be technically true but only just. It feels like almost the entirety of the game actively punishes you for daring to actually explore the environment with dead ends with nothing to find or gain. I managed to finish the game in 6 hours and that's with exploring the majority of the game environments only to be left high and dry for daring to play the game as it was described as the exploration game it was described as. There are literally two types of enemies in the game that you have to contest with and they're a slight inconvenience at worst with the soul exception of the ONE boss battle in the game.

Which leads me to the actual game play and story. This game is little more than an on rails "exploration" game in the sense that you're exploring precisely and only what the devs wanted you to explore. You're quite literally on rails for most of the game down long running tracks that are little more than run forward at speed with nothing to explore, see, or really do other than occasionally jumping. The plot itself is more or less mad scientist drunk with power in the most classic, cliche, and boring ways imaginable. Often times you've figured out the story elements well before the point that they've come out to literally spell them out to you. I have never had the feeling of hand holding this badly in a game before and it gets old incredibly fast. Finishing it in 6 hours was honestly being generous and frankly it could easily have been done in 4 hours.

[b]TL;DR:[/b]
Great visuals, audio, and movement physics, but the story and gameplay are often boring, and lack meaningful choices.

[hr]

[b]STORY[/b]

[list]

[*][b]The story could have actual twists and nuance[/b]

The twists in the story are predictable: the military scientist [spoiler]goes mad and builds super weapon, but you destroy it[/spoiler], the end.

Nature good.
Military bad.

You could have two flawed characters making compelling arguments:
- the scientist willing to sacrifice the environment, to [spoiler]give people immortality[/spoiler]
- the environmentalist willing to kill people, to save the environment
Then you choose who to help.

That could have been more interesting ending than [spoiler]destroying a giant laser.[/spoiler].


[*][b]The reveals that blue orbs [spoiler]are eggs[/spoiler] and they can be used to [spoiler]give people immortality[/spoiler] could have a payoff[/b]

These reveals occur and.... don't come up again.

It could have been great if they were utilised in the story, and tied into game play. E.g.
- using orbs or dying repeatedly leads to a “bad” ending, but preserving orbs leads to a “good” ending
- consuming orbs makes traversing faster, but makes nearby enemies aggressive


[*][b]The exposition dump could be cut[/b]

Act 1 starts with an exposition dump from a character you never hear from again. It could be easily replaced by environmental storytelling, or a leaked audio log from the scientist or environmentalist.


[*][b]We could discover the story[/b]

Your character finds dozens of audio logs in a mech suit and… doesn’t play them until the exact moment they’re relevant. It would be more sensical and fun to discover them at relevant moments.


[*][b]The repetitive, leading questions could be cut[/b]

Whenever a character asks a question. E.g. “Could this be sapping life from the environment?”
The unsaid answer is almost always: “Definitely yes, you idiot.”


[*][b]The protagonist’s inner monologue could be cut[/b]

Hearing the protagonist restate the obvious is grating, and robs players of self-insertion.


[*][b]The order of reveals could be improved[/b]

When I first saw [spoiler]spirits[/spoiler] I couldn’t tell whether they were considered mundane or exceptional. It needs to be established earlier.

The current story reveals: [spoiler]Spirits > mech suit > WW2 > ancient cultures teasers.[/spoiler]
It could be great if the order was: [spoiler]WW2 > mech suits > ancient culture teasers > spirits.[/spoiler]
[/list]

[hr]

[b]MOVEMENT[/b]

[list]
[*][b]Monotonous paths could be skilful[/b]

Roughly a twelfth of your time is spent moving in corridors, with an occasional jump, devoid of scenery or story.

Sometimes you are literally on rails. These segments were so repetitive and boring I closed my eyes and had my girlfriend tell me what to press. They’re unnecessary and make the world’s architecture nonsensical.

Simple fix: make rails cost energy, and cover their paths in energy pickups. Unlimited energy could still be an accessibility option.


[*][b]Monotonous paths could be optional[/b]

The mech suit offers several ways to traverse the environment, but you’re almost always forced to use one.

Most egregious example: after unlocking water-running, there’s water beside a wall… but you’re forced to slowly walk up the wall.

Most moments could allow at least two options.


[*][b]Hooks could be signposted, or a bonus[/b]

Often, if you’re unsure of where to go, it’s because there’s a hook above you that isn’t clearly signposted. It would be more fun if there were two ways out: a clear but slow path, and a hidden but quick hook.


[*][b]Water running could reward skill[/b]

It would be more engaging and thematic if water running costs energy, but is free while you have momentum.


[*][b]Wall walking could have been a choice, not a chore[/b]

The camera rotation is interesting the first time, but the slow speed makes it a chore. Wall walking (slow but free) would benefit from nearby alternatives: e.g. a hook point (fast, but costly and hidden).


[*][b]All movement abilities could be available immediately[/b]

It would make more narrative sense, and be more enjoyable (especially for replayability & speedrunning), if the mech started with all abilities unlocked.


[*][b]In summary, movement options could be:[/b]

[b]Forward[/b]
[b]Rails[/b] — Fast, costly, easy
[b]Water[/b] — Fast, costly*, easy (*free until you lose momentum)
[b]Walking[/b] — Slow, free, easy

[b]Upward[/b]
[b]Hooks[/b] — Fast, costly, easy* (*if you can spot them)
[b]Platforming[/b] — Slow, free, hard
[b]Wall walking[/b] — Super slow, free, easy

[b]Both[/b]
[b]Enemy-filled shortcuts[/b] — Fast, free, hard
[/list]

[hr]

[b]OTHER GAMEPLAY[/b]

[list]
[*][b]Death could be meaningful, or not promoted as a core feature[/b]

The marketing says your death affects the world, but it doesn’t. Trees change colour and shape. That’s it.


[*][b]We could actually discover mechanics[/b]

You play an archaeologist, but don’t get to discover breakthroughs. Movement “upgrades” are just sitting next to the first obstacle, with a tooltip.

Obstacles could appear earlier (but not usable until you have the upgrade), and tool tips could be replaced by optional logs or notes.


[*][b]“Threats” could be actual threats[/b]

Buildings go “critical” and collapse, but it has no game play effect. You’re entirely safe. Fires expanding or water rising would have been great. Invincibility could still be an accessibility option.


[*][b]Levels could be more polished[/b]

It’s often unclear what areas are intentional. Some have hidden goodies, others dead ends, invisible walls, or visible walls that let you outside the game.


[*][b]Dark areas could be brighter[/b]

Some areas are so dark it’s hard to progress without max brightness. Example: the rail cart section with nearly invisible mesh.


[*][b]Crates could be removed[/b]

Having to open crates and individually click loot is fiddly and repetitive. Rewards could just be auto-collected on collision.


[*][b]The notes could be replaced with audio logs[/b]

There’s a bunch of notes which would have worked better as audio logs.


[*][b]The currencies could be cut entirely[/b]

Coins: only open a temple, but upgrades are redundant once everything else is collected.
Acorns: only open doors, which feel like chores. Doors would be fine if optional (pay for shortcut vs traverse long way). 

Exploration could just reward acorns (for optional doors), or audio logs.


[*][b]The UI could be removed[/b]

Currencies — cut entirely
Energy / environment — displayed on suit
Objectives — cut, or in menu
Compass — navigating is easier when you just trust the level design


[*][b]A pacifist run could be possible[/b]

You don’t need to kill enemies to finish the game — which is great! You can choose slow/safe or quick/risky.

Sadly, one exception: you must kill the (only) boss. Pacifist run would be possible if escaping was an option (e.g. a difficult platforming area).
[/list]

И их всё равно в избытке.

Также тут очередной безликий, ничего не говорящий герой, никто, вешалка для костюма. Чего он туда полез?
